summary: Analyzes the solution space for route optimization in NEMO. With Basic Support, traffic must go through the mobile router and home agent tunnel, making routes longer and slower. This memo catalogs the types of route optimization that might be used. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If the mail detour is too long, there are different ways to shorten it. This note lists the different ideas and compares them.

subtitle: Analyzing different ways to optimize routes in mobile networks

tldr.problem: Network Mobility (NEMO) Basic Support creates sub-optimal routing, but many competing solution approaches exist with different tradeoffs in complexity, security, privacy, signaling overhead, and scope.
tldr.mechanism: The document classifies solutions into non-nested optimization (mobile router to correspondent entity), nested mobility optimization (reducing home agents or tunnels), infrastructure-based optimization, and intra-NEMO optimization. It then analyzes eight key design decisions: which entities participate, who initiates, how capability is detected, how addresses are represented, how addresses bind to locations, how signaling works, how data is transmitted, and security considerations.
tldr.outcome: This informational document maps the solution space to guide standardization efforts, showing that different approaches have fundamentally different strengths and weaknesses suitable for different deployment scenarios.

today: RFC 4889 remains an informational reference that describes the solution space without prescribing a specific approach. The NEMO working group later focused on specific solutions, such as RFC 5845 for mobile router position optimization and others addressing particular scenarios. The framework and questions raised in RFC 4889 remain relevant for evaluating new NEMO optimization proposals.

sections.title: The NEMO Route Optimization Challenge
sections.content:
RFC 4888 established that Network Mobility route optimization is needed. This document explores the vast solution space—the different types of approaches and design choices that could solve the problem. Since NEMO was first proposed, many different solutions have been suggested, each with different benefits and tradeoffs.

Solutions differ in which network entities participate, when optimization is initiated, how capabilities are detected, how mobile network node addresses are represented and bound to locations, how signaling is performed, how data packets are routed, and what security mechanisms protect them. This document classifies solutions by scenario and then analyzes each of these eight design questions to help the community understand the relative strengths and weaknesses of each approach.
sections.eli5: Many ideas exist for making the mail route shorter. This note analyzes what makes each idea work or fail.

sections.title: Benefits of Route Optimization
sections.content:
Route optimization brings clear benefits. Shorter routes reduce delay, improving quality of service for real-time applications and helping TCP perform better. Reduced network resource consumption comes from using fewer links, lowering congestion across the Internet. Reduced susceptibility to link failure occurs because shorter paths have fewer links to fail. Greater data efficiency comes from avoiding multiple levels of encapsulation, reducing header overhead and fragmentation.

Reduced processing delay results from eliminating multiple encapsulation and decapsulation operations. Avoiding home network bottlenecks allows traffic to bypass the home agent entirely. Avoiding security policy issues allows traffic from visiting mobile nodes to bypass home network security restrictions. Avoiding stalemate situations allows parent traffic to reach the Internet even when nested in a child mobile network, and allows direct communication between nodes in the same mobile network.
sections.eli5: Shorter mail routes are faster, use less space, break less often, and solve many problems created by always going through home.

sections.title: Scenarios and Solution Approaches
sections.content:
Non-nested optimization involves a mobile router or mobile network node establishing route optimization directly with a correspondent entity (node or router). The mobile router can send binding updates containing mobile network prefix information, allowing the correspondent entity to tunnel traffic directly to the mobile network without routing through the home agent.

Nested mobility optimization addresses cases where mobile IPv6 hosts are inside mobile networks or mobile routers attach to other mobile routers. Solutions either decrease the number of home agents on the path by bypassing some of them, or decrease the number of tunnels by collapsing nested tunneling.

Infrastructure-based optimization places the complexity in the network itself rather than at mobile nodes. Examples include proxy home agents that intercept and re-encapsulate traffic, or using distributed Mobility Anchor Points (MAPs) similar to hierarchical mobile IPv6.

Intra-NEMO optimization allows two mobile network nodes within the same nested network to communicate directly without routing outside the network, treating each other as correspondent entities or using ad-hoc routing.
sections.eli5: Solutions can optimize between routers and offices, between nested networks, hidden in infrastructure, or between neighbors in the same network.

sections.title: Design Challenges and Tradeoffs
sections.content:
Route optimization introduces significant challenges. Signaling overhead can create a signaling storm when networks change location, with a burst of binding updates overwhelming wireless links. Increased complexity in nodes and higher processing load can be problematic for resource-constrained mobile devices. Increased handoff delay occurs because route optimization procedures take longer than basic support.

Extending nodes with new functionality requires changes to mobile nodes, home agents, correspondent nodes, or infrastructure routers. Capability detection mechanisms may incur delays when nodes do not support optimization. Scalability issues arise when a single node must maintain many route optimization sessions. Mobility transparency may be compromised if mobile network nodes must be aware of their mobility. Location privacy is lost when correspondent nodes learn the mobile network's current location. Security challenges include verifying binding authenticity without pre-existing trust relationships. Legacy node support may be impossible if all routers in a nested network must implement the same solution.
sections.eli5: Smart routing creates complexity, delays, storms of signaling, privacy leaks, and compatibility nightmares that basic support avoids.

sections.title: Key Design Decisions in the Solution Space
sections.content:
Every route optimization solution must answer eight fundamental questions. Which entities participate? Solutions can involve mobile network nodes and correspondent nodes (most optimal but most complex), mobile routers and correspondent nodes, mobile routers and correspondent routers (preserving location privacy), or infrastructure-based entities. Who initiates optimization? The mobile node is usually in the best position to detect its movement, but in nested networks parent router mobility must be communicated to children.

How is capability detected? Nodes can attempt optimization and interpret the response, or use anycast queries or router alert options to detect correspondent routers. How is the address represented? Solutions can use mobile network prefixes (efficient for multiple nodes) or explicit node addresses (allows per-node control). How is the address bound to location? Binding can be to the parent mobile router's location (simple but incomplete for nested networks), to a sequence of upstream router locations (complete but complex), or to the root mobile router's location (flattens the network).

How is signaling performed? In-band signaling embeds information in data packets (responsive but overhead-heavy), while off-band signaling uses dedicated messages (cleaner but requires separate mechanism). How is data transmitted? Encapsulations create tunnels, routing headers contain sequences of intermediate points, or parent routers install routing table entries. What security is used? Return routability verification from Mobile IPv6 may suffice for single bindings but requires extensions for complex cases.
sections.eli5: Each solution picks from eight basic choices about who talks to whom, who starts, how they know it works, and how the magic happens.

sections.title: Security, Privacy, and Implementation Complexity
sections.content:
Security of address binding is critical. A correspondent entity must verify that binding updates claiming a mobile network prefix are authentic, preventing attacks where adversaries redirect traffic to themselves (snooping) or victims (denial-of-service). The standard Mobile IPv6 Return Routability procedure verifies collocated care-of and home addresses but does not verify prefix ownership. Extensions are needed for mobile network prefixes and sequences of upstream router locations.

End-to-end integrity is compromised when mobile routers act as proxies and must modify packets (inserting source addresses or routing headers) to achieve route optimization. This breaks security associations and prevents encrypted content inspection. Location privacy has three aspects: revealing the mobile network's location to the correspondent entity (unavoidable for optimization unless a correspondent router intermediates), the degree of revelation (full path with nested routers versus just the root router's location), and control over revelation (the mobile router versus the individual mobile network node).

Legacy node support varies: some approaches require all nodes to implement the same solution, while others allow incremental deployment. Implementation burden ranges from simple (reusing Mobile IPv6) to complex (new routing headers, modified signaling procedures, or infrastructure changes).
sections.eli5: Smart routing exposes location and breaks security unless carefully designed. Some ideas work only if everyone agrees, others need new cryptography, and all can break privacy if not careful.
